Two pulses pass through each other unchanged; at a fixed end a pulse comes back inverted.

Guided Inquiry

Two pulses on one string

A pulse of amplitude AL = +1 m travels to the right along a uniform string; a pulse of amplitude AR = −1 m travels to the left. Each faint curve is one pulse on its own, and the bright curve is the string's actual displacement y.

The instant the two pulses coincide

The two pulses are equal and opposite. At the instant one lies exactly on top of the other, what is the displacement of the string, and what happens after that?

Watch the crossing

Run it, and compare each pulse's height before the crossing with its height after. Then make both pulses upward and run it again.

A clamped end

The right end of the string is now clamped, so that point cannot move. A single upward pulse travels into the clamp. What travels back?

A second string instead of a clamp

The clamp is replaced by a second string tied on at the right end. For which second string does the reflected pulse come back inverted?

Two Pulses Meet

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Two pulses travel toward each other along a string. The sim draws each pulse, the string itself, and what happens when the right end is open, clamped or joined to a second string.

What you'll learn

  • How the shape of the string follows from the two pulses on it.
  • What each pulse looks like once the two have met and moved on.
  • How the reflection from the right end depends on what is there.
The opening setup: an upward pulse from the left, a downward pulse from the right.

What's on screen

  • Left pulse yL: the blue dashed curve, moving right.
  • Right pulse yR: the pink dotted curve, moving left. It is drawn only while the right end is open.
  • The string y: the bright amber curve, the string's actual displacement.
  • Right end: a plain continuation when open, a wall for a clamp, or a thicker or thinner line for a second string.
See itStart the opening setup. Watch for: the blue dashed and pink dotted pulses moving toward each other along the string.

Fixed: a 10 m string, pulse speed 2 m/s, pulse width 0.55 m, and a vertical scale of ±2 m. Each change restarts the run.

03

The string's displacement is the sum of the two pulses

At every point and every instant, the string's displacement is the sum of the displacements the two pulses would give there:

y(x, t) = yL(x, t) + yR(x, t)
The bright curve. It holds because the string is linear: the sim treats the displacements as small.
  • The pulses start 7.6 m apart and close at 4 m/s. Their centres meet at x = 5 m after 1.9 s.
  • With AL = +1 and AR = −1, the two displacements cancel at every point at that instant, and the string is flat.
  • The energy has not gone. The flat string is still moving, so at that instant all the energy is kinetic.
See itEqual and opposite pulses, AL = +1 and AR = −1. Watch for: the amber string lying flat on the dashed line at the 1.9 s meeting, under the banner "DISPLACEMENT = 0".
04

Each pulse leaves the meeting unchanged

After the meeting the pulses move apart again. Each keeps its own height, width and direction, as if the other had never been there.

  • At t = 3.8 s the left pulse, now near x = 8.8 m, is still +1 m high. The right pulse, now near x = 1.2 m, is still −1 m.
  • Cancelling is something that happens only while the pulses overlap. It does not change either pulse.
  • Pulses of the same sign add instead. With AL = AR = +1 the string reaches 2 m at x = 5 m, the largest value the two can make together. This is why the sim's scale runs to ±2 m.
  • Unequal pulses give a partial sum: AL = +1 and AR = +0.5 reach 1.5 m.
See itTwo upward pulses, AL = AR = +1. Watch for: the amber string reaching the +2 line at the meeting, then splitting into two 1 m pulses.
05

A clamped end sends the pulse back inverted

Choose Rigid clamp. A single pulse, AL, now travels into a fixed end at x = 10 m. The right pulse is not drawn. The clamp cannot move, so the string must stay at y = 0 there at every instant.

  • That is possible only if the returning pulse is flipped and the same height, so it cancels the arriving pulse at the wall. The sim draws exactly this.
  • The reflection coefficient is r = (v₂ − v₁)/(v₂ + v₁). A clamp is the limit v₂ → 0, giving r = −1 and a transmission τ = 0.
  • r = −1 means the whole pulse comes back, with a phase change of π. The readout shows −1.000 and "inverted (Δφ = π)".
  • Nothing enters the clamp, so all the energy returns.
See itA rigid clamp, one upward pulse with AL = +1. Watch for: a downward pulse of the same height leaving the clamp, and r = −1.000 in the readout.
06

A second string sets the sign and size of the reflection

Tie a second string on at x = 10 m, under the same tension. A heavier string carries waves more slowly. The first string has v₁ = 2 m/s. The heavier one has v₂ = 1 m/s and the lighter one v₂ = 4 m/s.

r = (v₂ − v₁)/(v₂ + v₁)
τ = 2v₂/(v₂ + v₁)
The reflected and the transmitted heights, as fractions of the incident height.
  • Heavier: r = −1/3, so the reflected pulse is inverted and a third of the height.
  • Lighter: r = +1/3, so the reflected pulse is upright and a third of the height.
  • The transmitted pulse is not drawn. The knot at the join rises to τAL: 0.67 m for the heavier string and 1.33 m for the lighter one.
See itA heavier string beyond, AL = +1. Watch for: r = −0.333 in the readout, and a small downward pulse coming back.
07

Where it matters

  • Voices in a room. Two people speaking at once are both heard. Their sound waves add where they overlap, and each wave carries on unchanged.
  • Noise-cancelling headphones. A wave opposite to the noise is added at the ear, so the sum there is small.
  • Ropes and strings. A pulse sent along a rope into a thicker rope comes partly back inverted. A guitar string is fixed at both ends, so its waves reflect inverted there.
08

Summary

In one line. This sim lets two pulses meet on a string, and puts a clamp or a second string at the right end, so you can see what each does to the pulses.

Key points

  • The string is y = yL + yR at every point and instant.
  • Each pulse leaves a meeting with its own height, width and direction.
  • A clamp gives r = −1: the pulse returns inverted, with all its energy.
  • A heavier second string gives r < 0, a lighter one r > 0.

Common mix-ups

  • "Equal and opposite pulses cancel for good." They cancel only while they overlap, and then each moves on.
  • "Cancelling destroys the energy." At the flat instant the energy is all kinetic.
  • "A wave always bounces back upright." It returns inverted from a clamp or from a heavier string.

Things to try on your own

  • Set AR to −0.5 and find the largest height of the string at the meeting.
  • Choose the lighter string and compare the reflected pulse with the heavier case.
